title: Stockholm Declaration
article: Declaration of the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment

definition.text: The Stockholm Declaration of 1972 was the first United Nations declaration on the global environment, a set of 26 principles agreed at the Stockholm Conference.

facts.text: Its first principle says people have a right to an environment of a quality that allows a life of dignity and well-being, and a duty to protect it for present and future generations.
It says Earth's capacity to produce vital renewable resources must be maintained and, where practicable, restored.
Principle 21, its legal core, gives states sovereign rights over their own territory along with a responsibility not to harm others across borders.
Developing countries argued that rich nations used most resources and caused most pollution, so the Global North should bear most of the responsibility.
Indira Gandhi's line that 'poverty is the worst form of pollution' framed a North–South divide that lasted for decades.
It is not legally binding; it counts as soft law, and critics called much of it too vague for legal use.
It shaped later treaties, and the 1992 Rio Declaration adopted a modified Principle 21.

definition.text: Earth Day is an annual event held on April 22 to show support for environmental protection, first held in 1970.

facts.text: US Senator Gaylord Nelson proposed a nationwide environmental teach-in for April 22, 1970, and hired the young activist Denis Hayes to coordinate it.
Nelson was moved to act after the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill, which released over 3 million US gallons of oil and killed more than 10,000 seabirds and sea mammals.
The 1970s that followed brought major US environmental laws such as the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act, the creation of the EPA, and bans on DDT and leaded gasoline.
In 1990 it went global, mobilizing 200 million people in 141 countries and helping pave the way for the 1992 Earth Summit.
The Paris Agreement was signed on Earth Day 2016 by leaders of 175 nations.
Nelson summed up the movement's view: 'The economy is a wholly owned subsidiary of the environment, not the other way around.'
